passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying doses of a novel drug on plasma concentration in healthy volunteers. Thirty participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group receiving a placebo, a low‑dose group receiving 10 mg, and a high‑dose group receiving 30 mg. Blood samples were collected 2 hours post‑dose and analyzed for drug concentration (µg/mL). The study aimed to assess dose‑dependent pharmacokinetics while balancing participant characteristics across groups through randomization. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers plan to use these findings to inform dose‑finding studies in patients with the target disease.
table_data:
Condition | N | Mean (µg/mL) | SD
Control | 10 | 5.2 | 0.8
Low Dose | 10 | 7.5 | 1.1
High Dose | 10 | 12.3 | 1.4
stem: Which experimental condition shows the greatest increase in mean plasma concentration relative to the control group?
explanation: The high‑dose group has a mean concentration of 12.3 µg/mL, which is higher than the control mean of 5.2 µg/mL, representing the largest absolute increase among the groups.
trap: Choosing the Control group because it is listed first, or Low Dose because it is the first increase, instead of the largest mean.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for inter‑individual variability in this study?
explanation: A crossover design allows each participant to receive multiple treatments in a randomized order, thereby controlling for inter‑individual differences by using participants as their own controls.
trap: Picking randomized controlled trial because the study was randomized, but only a crossover design uses each person as their own control.

stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the study design?

options.A: The standard deviation indicates variability within each group.
options.B: The mean concentration can be influenced by outliers.
options.C: A sample size of 10 is adequate to assume normality.
options.D: All data points contribute equally to the mean.

explanation: A sample size of 10 is generally considered small; it may not reliably satisfy the central limit theorem for normality, especially with potential outliers.
trap: Assuming n = 10 per group is enough to treat the data as normal, which a small sample cannot guarantee.

stem: The high-dose mean (12.3 µg/mL) exceeds the control mean (5.2 µg/mL) with n = 10 per group. What is needed to judge whether this 7.1 µg/mL difference is larger than expected by chance?

options.A: A statistical test comparing the two means that uses the group SDs and sample sizes
options.B: The range of the control group alone
options.C: The ratio of the doses (30 mg : 10 mg)

explanation: Correct: A) Whether a difference in means exceeds chance variation depends on the spread (SD) and sample size, which is what a hypothesis test for two means uses. Why the others are wrong: B) the control range ignores the high-dose group and the sample size. C) the dose ratio says nothing about sampling variability. D) a percent increase gives the size of the difference, not whether it exceeds chance.
trap: Treating a large percent increase as proof of a real difference without considering variability and sample size.
